title: Risi e Bisi
subtitle: Venetian rice and peas
excerpt: Risi e bisi is a Venetian rice and pea dish that sits between a risotto and a thick soup. It is made in spring when fresh peas are in season and is traditionally served on 25 April, the feast of Saint Mark, patron of Venice. The pea pods are used to make the stock, giving the dish an intense green, sweet flavour.
sourceNotes: Risi e bisi is one of the oldest recorded Venetian dishes, appearing in chronicles of the Doge's feasts from the fifteenth century onward. It was the prestige dish served to the Doge on 25 April, the feast of Saint Mark. The dish uses the pea pods to make stock, a technique that maximises the flavour of fresh peas.

content.text: Risi e bisi is not quite a risotto and not quite a soup: it should be looser and more liquid than a risotto but not pourable. The classic technique uses the pea pods to make a simple stock, which is then used to cook the rice. If pods are unavailable, use good chicken stock instead. Fresh peas in season give a sweeter result, but frozen peas work well.

Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} of olive oil in a heavy pan over a medium heat. Add {{pancetta}} pancetta and cook until lightly golden, about 3 minutes. Add {{onion}} onion and cook gently for 8 minutes until soft.

Add {{carnaroli-rice}} rice and stir for 2 minutes. Add the hot {{chicken-stock}} stock a ladleful at a time, stirring and waiting for each addition to absorb. After 10 minutes, add {{peas-frozen}} peas and continue adding stock for a further 8 minutes until the rice is just tender. The texture should be quite loose -- add more stock if needed.

Remove from the heat. Stir in {{unsalted-butter}} butter and {{parmesan}} Parmesan. Add {{parsley-flat}} parsley. Season with {{salt-table}} salt and {{black-pepper}} pepper. Rest for 2 minutes, then serve in deep bowls.

items.cause: The rice absorbed more stock than expected, or the pan was too wide.
items.fix: Risi e bisi should be thinner than a risotto. Stir in hot stock or hot water a ladleful at a time until the right consistency is reached -- it should flow slowly when the pan is tilted.

content.text: Risi e bisi is one of the oldest dishes in the Venetian canon. It was the dish served at the Doge's table on 25 April each year, the feast of Saint Mark. Only the first peas of the season from the island of Sant'Erasmo in the Venice lagoon were used. The dish sits between a risotto and a minestra and is listed under both in old Venetian cookery books. Outside Venice it is less well known than Milanese or Parmesan risotto, which is a shame.
